frameworks.name: SCALE Loop
frameworks.definition: A five-step loop for growing any system or department: Start (begin), Compound (do more volume), Augment (do better), Leverage (automate for consistency), Expand (move to next channel or territory).

frameworks.name: Question-Delete-Optimize-Timelines-Automate (Turnaround Sequence)
frameworks.definition: A five-step optimization sequence for fixing an existing broken system: question every requirement, delete everything non-essential, optimize remaining work by output-per-resource, pull up timelines, then automate.

frameworks.name: Six Horsemen of Business Stagnation
frameworks.definition: Six structural reasons businesses get stuck: (1) underpriced, (2) overcompensation of employees, (3) serving too many avatars, (4) overextension into multiple locations or businesses, (5) running more than one business without focus, (6) no data collection.

frameworks.name: B2B Brand Building Buckets
frameworks.definition: Three approaches for building a B2B brand without celebrity endorsements: (1) help your audience accomplish their goals for free (content), (2) demonstrate success for people like them (case studies/proof), (3) accomplish an aspirational outcome yourself.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that short-horizon planning (12-week windows with at most one or two annual targets) outperforms detailed long-range plans because conditions change so fast that plans made 12 months prior are typically half-irrelevant by the time they are reviewed.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to fast-moving businesses where market conditions shift year-over-year
claims.mechanism: Long-range plans are built on hundreds of variables that cannot be known in advance; by the time the plan is executed, many assumptions have already been invalidated by changed conditions.
bounded_by: Jensen Huang of NVIDIA cited as corroborating example for 30+ year company horizon

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that concentrating all available resources on a single priority domino, rather than splitting effort across five parallel priorities, results in faster completion of all objectives because solving the top constraint unblocks downstream tasks automatically.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies when the organization has a genuine constraint or leverage point that affects multiple downstream outcomes
claims.mechanism: When all resources align on one problem, it is solved faster; solving that one problem removes blockers that were independently slowing B, C, D, and E, so those cascade faster than if all five were attacked simultaneously.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that for a meta-ads agency, investing in brand building resolves lead volume, show-up rate, and close rate problems simultaneously, making brand the single domino that collapses the entire problem set.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: small B2B agency running paid ads for clients
currently struggling with leads, show-up rate, and close rate simultaneously
claims.mechanism: A warm brand audience produces inbound leads without ads, raises show-up rates because prospects already trust the brand, and increases close rates because conversations are already pre-sold.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that supply-constrained service businesses (cleaning, accounting, legal, high-end consulting) should recognize that their real business is attracting, hiring, training, managing, and incentivizing supply-side talent, because demand for these services is largely self-sustaining.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service businesses where customers are abundant but qualified providers are scarce
claims.mechanism: When demand takes care of itself, the binding constraint is always on the supply side; any growth dollar spent on demand generation yields negligible return relative to dollars spent attracting and retaining providers.
bounded_by: does not apply to demand-constrained businesses such as e-commerce, B2B SaaS, or weight loss products where competitors supply far exceeds demand

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that demand-constrained businesses (e-commerce, B2B SaaS, consumer weight loss, music lessons) face the opposite problem: finding customers is their hardest challenge, not finding providers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: markets where competitors or substitutes are abundant relative to paying customers
bounded_by: supply-demand curve shifts dynamically over time; a category that is demand-constrained today may become supply-constrained as the market matures

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that business owners in supply-constrained businesses dramatically underpay for talent recruitment relative to the gross profit that each competent employee generates, and that referral bonuses of 20% of the annual gross profit per hire are economically justified.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: supply-constrained service businesses where each additional competent hire generates predictable recurring gross profit
claims.mechanism: Treating a new hire as a yield-bearing asset: if a plumber generates $400,000 in annual gross profit, paying $50,000-$80,000 to acquire that hire is a 5-8x return in year one alone, making high referral bonuses economically rational.

numbers.axis: referral bonus justification relative to employee annual gross profit

anchors.value: any bonus less than one month of GP forgone from delayed hire

bounded_by: risk of hire leaving early must be discounted against the bonus amount; but Hormozi argues owners discount too aggressively given the opportunity cost of the delay

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the single largest shift in his understanding of business in 2025 was recognizing that attracting and retaining top talent is the highest-leverage activity available to a CEO, and that the CEOs of the best-performing companies (Apple, Amazon, Meta) all take a direct, active role in recruiting top talent.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to scaling businesses where quality of leadership talent determines growth ceiling
claims.mechanism: Top talent cannot be attracted through traditional recruiters because they are already successful and will only respond to direct engagement from a founder or CEO who demonstrates personal interest and aligned incentives.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that founders who work more hours produce disproportionately more output than those who work fewer hours, because working prevents spending (a double positive swing) and full immersion in the problem compounds faster than intermittent engagement.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to founders optimizing for financial wealth as the primary outcome
claims.mechanism: Working more creates a positive swing twice: income rises while spending falls because there is no time to spend; additionally, sustained immersion builds pattern recognition and context that intermittent workers do not accumulate, similar to how children who take three months off school lose roughly a quarter of the year re-acquiring prior knowledge.

numbers.axis: hours worked per week during high-growth phases

anchors.value: ~90 hours/week (7 days, 12h average with 2-3 days at 18h)

anchors.region: days off in first 100 days of year

bounded_by: Hormozi explicitly notes this is personal preference and does not prescribe it for others; social support from spouse and integration of personal life into work environment are preconditions for his specific setup

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a business owner at full capacity who is not making money is almost always underpriced, and that the correct fix is to raise price incrementally using a 5-and-20 rule until conversion drops.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service business at or near full capacity with insufficient profit margin
claims.mechanism: Full capacity with no margin proves demand exists at current price; raising price reduces volume slightly but increases revenue and reduces service cost simultaneously, creating a disproportionate profit increase because both revenue rises and costs fall.

anchors.region: sell 5 customers at current price with normal conversion
continue until net revenue stops increasing
anchors.value: stop signal: conversion drops enough that total take is lower
fewer clients to service = lower cost + higher revenue = disproportionate profit increase

bounded_by: harder to execute when sales volume is low (e.g., 1-2 deals per month) because the brain processes each no as binary failure rather than calculating the net revenue gain

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that overcompensating key employees (through accidental revenue share arrangements made when revenue was low) creates a structural cap on growth, and the fix requires first building replacement capacity before renegotiating terms, to negotiate from strength rather than desperation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service businesses where early revenue share arrangements persist after revenue has grown significantly beyond original projections
claims.mechanism: Attempting to renegotiate compensation without a ready replacement gives the employee leverage to hold the business hostage; bringing in a replacement first creates negotiating parity, allowing the renegotiation conversation to be held from a position of strength with a credible fallback.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that serving too many customer avatars prevents getting offer, messaging, and advertising right, and that applying 80-20 analysis to existing customers to identify the top 20% and then pricing and messaging exclusively for them is the correct resolution.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: businesses under ~$3M revenue that are stagnating due to incoherent messaging and offer
claims.mechanism: A narrow avatar enables specific messaging that attracts more of the right people; pricing can reflect the full value delivered to that narrow group rather than being averaged down across a mixed audience, producing higher margin per sale.

numbers.axis: revenue stage at which avatar dilution is most common constraint

anchors.value: identify top 20% of existing customers and rebuild offer exclusively for them

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that overextension into multiple locations or businesses before the first unit is independently operable is one of the most common causes of stagnation, and that the correct test is whether the business maintains or grows for six straight months without the founder's direct involvement.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service or brick-and-mortar businesses with $1M-$3M revenue considering second location or business
claims.mechanism: When a founder leaves to open the second location, their operational contribution to the first location is revealed; if the first location declines, it proves the founder was the CEO, not just the owner, and the business was not independently operable.

anchors.value: six straight months of maintenance or growth without founder direct involvement

bounded_by: the six-month test is invalid if the founder continues working in the day-to-day during the test period under a different label

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that running more than one business simultaneously is a structural stagnation trap, because the opportunity in any business lies in solving the unsolved problems, and splitting attention across two businesses means neither set of problems gets solved.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founders operating two or more businesses concurrently without a clear operator for each
claims.mechanism: The opportunity in any business is not missed opportunities but unsolved problems; unsolved problems require dedicated attention, which a split-focus founder cannot provide; sunk cost fallacy causes founders to delay choosing.
bounded_by: does not apply to holding companies with professional operators running each entity independently

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that not collecting data on key business metrics (lead cost, close rate, churn) is the sixth horseman of stagnation, but unlike the first five, it has no meaningful short-term downside to fixing; the only constraint is opportunity cost of not doing shinier things instead.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any business where core funnel metrics are not tracked

claims.text: Alex Hormozi proposes a data-value test: a metric is worth tracking only if a change (up or down) would change the business's behavior; metrics that do not alter decisions should not be tracked regardless of availability.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any business deciding which metrics to instrument
claims.mechanism: Unlimited variables can be tracked; tracking cost is not zero (time, attention, dashboards); only metrics that are inputs to decisions justify their tracking cost.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that problems in a business are finite and enumerable, while missed opportunities are infinite; a founder who focuses on missed opportunities instead of problems will perpetually start new half-built bridges and never cross any of them.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Problems are the real constraint on business growth; missed opportunities have infinite supply but infinite distraction cost; solving one real problem compounds the business, while starting one missed opportunity simply adds another incomplete project.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that urgency (rush) in a business context is entirely a function of who a founder chooses to compare themselves against, and therefore is arbitrary and self-generated rather than externally imposed.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to founders in markets without winner-take-all network effects
claims.mechanism: In winner-take-all markets (Uber, Apple, Android), there is genuine urgency because there are only two market positions. In the 99% of markets without network effects, the only urgency driver is arbitrary comparison reference points that the founder selects.
bounded_by: does not apply to network-effect businesses where genuine winner-take-all dynamics create real first-mover urgency

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that New Balance's CMO shifted the ad spend ratio from 70% bottom-of-funnel/30% top-of-funnel to 30% bottom/70% top, saw revenue decline for 18 months, and then experienced a significant inflection upward, suggesting brand investment has an approximately 18-month payback lag at scale.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: large consumer brand with significant ad budget; results may not generalize to smaller businesses with shorter feedback loops
claims.mechanism: Brand awareness (top-of-funnel) builds associations and trust over time; the 18-month delay reflects the time required for brand impressions to compound into changed consumer behavior and purchase decisions.

numbers.axis: top-of-funnel vs bottom-of-funnel ad spend ratio and timeline to revenue inflection

bounded_by: Hormozi notes this reflects New Balance's budget scale; smaller businesses may see different lag times

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a 3:1 content-to-ask ratio (three value-giving impressions before each request or advertisement) is the structural requirement for maintaining a brand channel that audiences continue to engage with, as evidenced by television and radio industry research.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to content-based audience building on social media, YouTube, or any media channel
claims.mechanism: If the ratio drops below 3:1 (e.g., to 2:1), audiences exit the channel; the 3:1 threshold reflects the human tolerance for advertising interruption relative to value delivery.

anchors.value: every 4th post in newsfeed is an ad (3:1 ratio)

bounded_by: Hormozi references television and radio industry research; applicability to newer platforms with algorithmic feeds may differ

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that in-person (IRL) customer experiences produce materially higher brand affinity, loyalty, referral rates, ratings, and repeat purchase frequency than digital-only interactions, and that the demand for in-person connection is structurally under-supplied post-COVID.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Digital connections are a false substitute for genuine in-person connection; the analogy is fake food that keeps you full without satisfying; real in-person experiences generate emotional associations that digital touchpoints cannot replicate at equal depth.
bounded_by: Hormozi acknowledges IRL experiences are harder to scale; argues that the difficulty of scaling increases their defensibility as a moat

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a spouse or partner who actively discourages work, distracts the entrepreneur, and incentivizes leisure is a material negative input on business outcomes, comparable in effect to a competitor trying to undermine performance, even without malicious intent.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: entrepreneurs in high-growth phases requiring discretionary effort
claims.mechanism: A partner controls the home environment; a partner who diverts discretionary time toward leisure and away from business reduces the total hours of high-quality work available; partners who reinforce work and absorb household friction have the opposite effect.
bounded_by: Hormozi explicitly states he is not imputing malicious intent; the effect on outcomes is the claim, not a moral judgment

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when optimizing a department, pulling up timelines by converting weekly deadlines to daily deadlines can multiply team output speed by as much as 7x, because teams default to filling available time rather than compressing work to minimum required duration.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: knowledge-work teams with recurring deliverables on weekly cadences
claims.mechanism: If a team delivers a report to a Monday meeting, converting the deadline to end-of-current-day compresses execution from 7 days to 1 day; the underlying task does not require 7 days of work, it simply expands to fill the available window (Parkinson's Law).
bounded_by: requires future capacity to be available for the freed time; Hormozi's argument is that future priority spikes always emerge, so unused current capacity should be consumed proactively

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that conversion rate optimization (CRO) run as a continuous discipline (3-10 active split tests on key revenue touchpoints at any time) produces compounding returns because efficiency gains are durable and expand LTV-to-CAC ratios, enabling increased spend in advertising and talent.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: businesses with sufficient traffic volume to run statistically valid split tests
claims.mechanism: Unlike revenue growth (which may be temporary), conversion rate improvements are durable; a higher conversion rate permanently lowers effective CAC and raises LTV, which expands the range of viable acquisition channels and talent investments.

numbers.axis: CRO wins achieved in a single company within one portfolio

anchors.value: approximately 100 split tests to find 3 winners

bounded_by: requires sufficient traffic to achieve statistical significance; the example company was eight figures-plus per month in revenue

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that for a B2B business, building brand through educational content, documented proof for customers like the target, and aspirational outcomes achieved by the founder directly are the three available brand-building levers when celebrity athlete endorsement is not feasible.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: B2B businesses without celebrity endorsement access; contrasts with CPG brand playbook
bounded_by: the direct-response-to-brand transition requires accepting 12-18 months of declining short-term returns before the inflection occurs

examples.text: Alex Hormozi describes advising a home services company that was turning away plumbing business because they could not find enough plumbers. The company was generating $400,000 in annual gross profit per plumber. Hormozi asked what they would pay one time for a recurring $400,000 annual income stream and compared it to buying a stock with that yield. The answer was that if properly framed as a capital investment with a discount for attrition risk, the company should be willing to pay $80,000-$100,000 per plumber hire. Instead, the company was offering a $1,000 referral bonus. The gap between $1,000 and the economically justified number illustrates how severely business owners underprice supply-side talent acquisition.

Alex Hormozi recounts a portfolio company that had a downsell offer that almost no one purchased. He asked whether they had considered giving it away for free as a lead magnet. They implemented this and tripled lead flow the following week. The downsell had been worth approximately 5% of revenue; tripling lead flow cut CAC by two-thirds and roughly tripled the business's top line. This example illustrates how one reframing of an underperforming asset can unlock a multiplier across the entire business.

Alex Hormozi describes inheriting a media team, canceling all recurring meetings and one-on-ones on day one, and replacing them with a single daily huddle. His reasoning was that content creators are deep workers and any interruption to flow state disproportionately impacts their performance. After deletion, he then added back only the meetings that proved their value through demonstrated output impact. This example illustrates the question-delete-optimize-timelines-automate turnaround sequence applied to a creative department.

Alex Hormozi recounts that Acquisition.com's workshops division was created from excess capacity: an open floor of unused desks in their headquarters and a portfolio team that had bandwidth between portfolio engagements. By inviting businesses to fly in for two-day workshops, they generated deal flow, cash flow, content, and talent relationships simultaneously, all without adding net cost. The sawdust that created this division was the existing building lease and the existing team payroll.

Alex Hormozi recounts spending time with Ben Francis (Gymshark CEO) and Noel Mack (Gymshark Head of Brand), who connected him with New Balance's CMO. The CMO had inherited a plateaued brand, requested permission to flip the ad spend ratio from 70% bottom-of-funnel to 70% top-of-funnel, watched revenue decline for 18 months, and then saw a significant inflection upward that drove New Balance's brand resurgence. Hormozi uses this story to illustrate both the 3:1 give-to-ask ratio and the 18-month payback lag for brand investment.

Alex Hormozi describes the experience of visiting a luxury resort with only 22 villas and having no emotional response to the beauty of the surroundings. He realized that his enjoyment of vacations had been socially programmed by others whose lifestyle preferences he was inadvertently adopting. This led him to conclude that mandatory vacations are not universal human requirements and that his natural preference is continuous work because it generates his desired outcomes. He took 10-12 total days off in 2025.

Alex Hormozi explains his personal Big Money Ideas list. When a new opportunity occurs to him, instead of acting on it or sharing it, he writes it down in detail on the list. When the team has genuine bandwidth, he reviews the list and picks the highest-leverage item. He notes that many ideas he was passionate about one month look unimportant two months later, meaning the cooling period filters out shiny-object impulses before they consume team resources.

practices.text: When diagnosing a business constraint, first determine whether it is supply-constrained or demand-constrained before choosing any tactical response.
For supply-constrained businesses, build an internal employee referral program with bonuses calibrated to a meaningful percentage of the annual gross profit that each new hire generates.
When taking over a broken department, start by deleting all meetings, then add back only those that prove their value through output impact.
Use end-of-day rather than end-of-week deadlines for all recurring deliverables to compress execution timelines and free future bandwidth for unexpected priorities.
Before acting on a new opportunity or idea, write it down in detail in a designated list and let it sit for at least a month; act only on items that survive the cooling period.
Apply 80-20 analysis to your customer base, identify the top 20% by profitability or value delivered, and rebuild your offer and messaging exclusively for that group.
When considering any new division, product, or initiative, ask whether it checks multiple boxes (deal flow, cash flow, content, talent flow) at no additional net cost before committing.
Run 3-10 split tests simultaneously on every high-traffic revenue touchpoint at all times as a standing discipline, not a one-off project.
Before hiring a key executive, gauge the support level of their spouse or partner; prioritize candidates whose home environment actively reinforces their professional ambition.
When someone on your team says 'we can't do that,' redirect to 'what would it take?' to force backward planning from the desired outcome rather than forward planning from current constraints.
